title: Land Rover Defender (L663)
verdict: The Defender that shares nothing with the Defender: an aluminium monocoque on independent air springs that will out-climb its ancestor and then massage your back on the way home. Brilliant off-road, a little too clever for its own good in the workshop.

paragraphs: The L663 is the argument that ended an argument. For years, purists insisted a Defender needed a ladder frame and beam axles. Land Rover built one with neither, gave it permanent four-wheel drive, a two-speed transfer box, locking differentials and 900 mm of wading depth, and sold it in America again. It is quicker, safer, quieter and more capable than the truck it replaced. It is also a modern JLR, which means the things that go wrong are sensors, software and converters rather than swivel seals.

story.heading: BREAKING THE LINEAGE
paragraphs: Land Rover showed its hand early with the DC100 concept at the 2011 Frankfurt Motor Show, a 100-inch-wheelbase sketch of a modern Defender. The production truck, styled under Gerry McGovern, was unveiled at Frankfurt on 10 September 2019. It was the first all-new Defender since 1983 and, by Land Rover's account, shares no components or technology with its predecessor: the body is an aluminium monocoque on JLR's D7x platform, and the live axles are gone in favour of all-round independent suspension.

Production moved too. The L663 is built at JLR's plant in Nitra, Slovakia, which opened on 25 October 2018. Deliveries of the five-door 110 began in early 2020, the three-door 90 followed late that year, and the 130 later kept the 110's wheelbase but added a longer rear overhang for eight seats. For the [[land-rover/defender-90-110|classic Defender]] faithful in the US, the more important news was simpler: after the NAS trucks left in 1997, Land Rover was selling a Defender here again.

story.heading: WHAT IT CAN ACTUALLY DO
paragraphs: The hardware list reads like a checklist written by someone who'd been told it would be soft. Permanent four-wheel drive through a ZF eight-speed automatic and a two-speed transfer case, a bevel-gear centre differential splitting torque 50/50 that you can lock, and a locking rear differential. Every 110 rides on air suspension, which lifts it to 291 mm of ground clearance; the 90 can have coils (226 mm) or air. Land Rover quotes 900 mm (35.4 in) of wading depth, and Wade Sensing uses the cameras to show you how deep you are.

It is a working truck in the numbers that matter to overlanders, too. Land Rover quotes up to 3,500 kg of towing in the UK and up to 8,200 lb in the US, a 300 kg (661 lb) static roof load for a rooftop tent, and up to 370 lb of dynamic roof load on the 110 and 130 with off-road tyres and the Expedition Roof Rack. Unusually for a unibody, a 4,536 kg load-rated front winch is officially supported. Off-road it simply walks up things the [[land-rover/series|Series]] trucks would have had to winch.

story.heading: ENGINES, V8S AND THE OCTA
paragraphs: Engines are JLR's Ingenium family: a 2.0 turbo petrol P300, a 3.0 mild-hybrid straight-six P400, a P400e plug-in hybrid for the 110, and in Europe and Australia a run of diesels, first 2.0 four-cylinders and then 3.0 mild-hybrid sixes badged D200, D250, D300 and later D350. From 2021 the supercharged 5.0 V8 P525 added 518 bhp, and 300 all-black V8 Bond Editions marked the truck's role in No Time to Die.

Then Land Rover went further. The OCTA, announced in July 2024, uses BMW's 4.4-litre twin-turbo mild-hybrid V8 with 635 PS (626 hp in US trim) and claims 0–60 mph in 3.8 seconds. It gets hydraulically interlinked 6D Dynamics suspension, sits wider and higher than a standard Defender, and fits 33-inch tyres from the factory. Land Rover has since taken a rally-raid Defender, the D7X-R, to the Dakar, and says it won on its 2026 debut. The [[g-class/second-gen|G-Class]] now has a genuine rival on every surface.

story.heading: LIVING WITH IT
paragraphs: The motoring press loved the new truck; owners have been more mixed. A TFL review collected reader accounts of faults within the first few hundred miles, and Defender2.net's L663 Faults & Fixes board is busy with DC-DC converter failures on mild hybrids, DPF and EGR sensor codes on the diesels, steering knocks and recall campaigns. None of it is the stuff you fix with a 13 mm spanner in a field, and an independent diagnostic tool has become as common an accessory as a roof rack.

The 26MY facelift, unveiled on 28 May 2025, brought flush lights and a 13.1-inch screen but left the structure alone. In September 2026 the Defender Wolf Series II, built on the same D7x platform, was launched to bid for the UK Ministry of Defence's Light Mobility Vehicle tender, putting the name back where the [[land-rover/series|Series]] started. If you want the old recipe of separate chassis and beam axles, the [[grenadier/station-wagon|Ineos Grenadier]] exists precisely because this truck abandoned it.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · SPECIAL EDITIONS
callout.title: Bond cars, Camel yellow and a Lego Defender
paragraphs: The Bond Edition (2021) was 300 V8 Defenders in all black with 22-inch black wheels, blue calipers and 'Defender 007' badging, priced from £105,000. The 75th Anniversary Edition was painted Grasmere Green as a nod to HUE 166, the first pre-production Land Rover. The Trophy Edition, in Deep Sandglow Yellow or Keswick Green, is a homage to the Camel Trophy that the classic 110 made famous.

For North America, the 2023 30th Anniversary Edition was a 500-unit run of Fuji White Defender 110 P300s on white steel wheels with the Expedition roof rack and side ladder, marking 30 years since the NAS 110. And if you can't afford any of them, Lego's 2,573-piece Defender set of October 2019 is one of the largest sets it has made.

engineering_intro: The L663 throws out the ladder frame entirely. Its aluminium monocoque (JLR's D7x platform) carries independent suspension at all four corners, air-sprung on every 110 and optional on the 90, which gets coils as standard. Drive is permanent through a ZF eight-speed automatic and a two-speed transfer case with a lockable 50/50 centre differential and a locking rear differential. Off-road capability comes as much from software (Terrain Response 2, All-Terrain Progress Control, Wade Sensing) as from hardware, which is both why it is so good and why owners carry diagnostic tools.

engineering.note: No separate chassis; integrated body and frame.
Air standard on the 110; the 90 offers coils or air.

buying_checks.head: Recall and campaign status
buying_checks.body: Have a dealer or diagnostic tool confirm every open campaign is closed. Owners on Defender2.net report an airbag recall and the E005 campaign for 3.0 Ingenium diesels built between 1 March 2024 and 18 April 2026, where the auxiliary belt idler pulley can damage the oil pressure and temperature sensor, causing an oil leak and possible stalling.

buying_checks.head: Oil-change history
buying_checks.body: The headline service interval is long, and some trucks reach their first service on the original oil. Defender2.net members note the oil-change interval is driven by a separate condition-based counter and many owners change oil every 7,000–10,000 miles. A truck with only dealer visits at 21,000-mile intervals deserves a closer look.

buying_checks.head: DC-DC converter (mild hybrids)
buying_checks.body: MHEV trucks have suffered DC-DC converter failures, with owners reporting waits of two weeks to two months for parts. Ask whether it has been replaced and whether the relevant software updates are done.

buying_checks.head: Diesel DPF and sensor codes
buying_checks.body: Frequent regenerations (every 35–100 miles) and codes such as P24C6/P24C7 (PM sensor temperature) or P0401 (EGR flow) are documented on the diesels. Scan for stored codes and ask about regeneration frequency before buying a high-mileage D250/D300.

buying_checks.head: Steering knock on rough roads
buying_checks.body: Several owners report knocking through the steering on corrugations, traced variously to the lower steering-column UJ, track rod ends, front lower control arms or a replacement steering rack under warranty. Wiggle the wheel at a standstill and listen.

buying_checks.head: Coolant loss (P400)
buying_checks.body: Petrol six-cylinder owners report coolant loss from turbo coolant line O-rings, leaky expansion tanks and stone-damaged auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes. Check the level cold and look for crusty residue.

buying_checks.head: Coil or air, and which body
buying_checks.body: Every 110 is on air; a 90 can be either. Coil 90s ride and tow fine but don't have the air trucks' height adjustment (no Access mode), and the 290 mm-plus clearance figure is for air.

repairs.title: Engine oil and filter (3.0 Ingenium diesel)
repairs.symptoms: Due on the oil-life counter, or you want shorter intervals than the factory schedule.
repairs.fix: Drain through the sump plug: remove the two underbody shields (and any aftermarket front guard) to reach it. Defender2.net owners report refills of about 8.5–8.8 litres for the 3.0 diesel; one used 0W-30 to JLR spec 03-5007 with a new filter. Extraction through the dipstick tube works but the tube catches on ledges in the block, so mark the depth on your probe. Reset the oil service counter afterwards with a diagnostic tool, or the truck won't know it has fresh oil.
repairs.tools: Sockets for the undertray, sump plug socket, filter tool, extractor (optional), diagnostic tool such as a GAP IIDTool · 0W-30 to JLR 03-5007 · oil filter

repairs.title: Lower steering shaft joint and gaiter
repairs.symptoms: Split rubber boot on the lower steering shaft, often spotted on weekly checks or flagged at MOT, sometimes with a knock through the wheel.
repairs.fix: The joint is held by two bolts; the upper section slides up to release it. A member quotes the workshop manual as calling for new bolts torqued to 30 Nm. You can fit just the boot if the joint is good, but it's awkward; replacing the joint assembly is easier.
repairs.tools: Sockets, torque wrench · joint LR033648 (RHD) or LR033647 (LHD), bolts QYG500090 and LR116214 per Defender2.net

repairs.title: PM sensor for P24C6 / P24C7
repairs.symptoms: Engine light after cold starts, codes P24C6/P24C7 (particulate matter sensor temperature circuit), and regenerations every 100 miles or so.
repairs.fix: One owner of a 2022 D250 replaced the PM temperature sensor, the last sensor in the exhaust after the DPF. After a week of cold starts and about 150 miles the light hadn't returned and short-trip regenerations stopped. Clear the codes afterwards.
repairs.tools: Sensor socket, penetrating oil, diagnostic tool · Bosch 0281008520 per Defender2.net (another member cross-references LR146856)

repairs.title: Chase a P0401 EGR flow fault
repairs.symptoms: Judder and hesitation at low-speed acceleration, especially on 1–2 and 2–3 shifts, then P0401 (EGR flow insufficient) and sometimes P006B.
repairs.fix: Log demanded versus actual EGR valve position with a diagnostic tool. In one documented 3.0 diesel case, the dealer replaced the inlet manifold pressure sensor but the fault returned. A member pointed to the exhaust pressure sensor in the 90-degree bend just after the turbo, whose narrow pipe can block with soot and confuse the EGR logic. If the valve itself is sticking, clean or replace it; short-trip use makes this worse.
repairs.tools: Diagnostic tool with live data, sockets · exhaust pressure sensor pipe, EGR valve (as diagnosed)

parts.name: Exhaust gas pressure sensor (search, confirm fitment)

repairs.title: Coolant loss on the P400
repairs.cost: One Australian owner paid AU$580 (about $320 parts, $260 labour)
repairs.symptoms: Coolant dropping from max to min within 100–150 km with no obvious puddle.
repairs.fix: Pressure-test the system, then check the turbo coolant feed and return lines (their O-rings are a known leak), the expansion tank and its level sensor, and the auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes for stone damage. Replace the leaking lines with new seals and refill and bleed.
repairs.tools: Cooling-system pressure tester, sockets · turbo coolant lines and O-rings, coolant to spec

repairs.title: Track rod end for a random clunk
repairs.symptoms: Metallic clunk when steering or when the suspension articulates, at no particular angle.
repairs.fix: Check bushes and the track rod ends before assuming a wheel bearing. One owner traced the noise to a track rod end: count the threads to keep the toe close, split the taper with a ball-joint splitter (the hardest part of the job), fit the new end and get the alignment checked.
repairs.tools: Ball-joint splitter, spanners, torque wrench · track rod end

parts.name: Track rod end (search, confirm L663 fitment)

repairs.title: Re-bond lifting wheel-arch extensions
repairs.cost: Price of tape and adhesion promoter
repairs.symptoms: The outer edge of a dealer-fitted arch extension peeling away from the body.
repairs.fix: The extensions' outer edge is held by double-sided tape, so most failures are preparation. Remove the extension, clean both surfaces thoroughly, use adhesion promoter and refit with fresh tape; a member suggests 3M VHB-type foam mounting tape.
repairs.tools: Trim tools, cleaner, adhesion promoter · 3M 5925 VHB tape (25 mm)

parts.name: LR130587 front wheel arch moulding, LH, New Defender L663

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: 275/60R20 (about 33 inches) is the popular step up from the factory 255/60R20. A Defender2.net owner fitted it to a coil-sprung 110 on stock 8.5-inch 20s with no spacers and reports no rubbing, even off-road; others warn it can touch on some setups. 275/55R20 runs without rubbing on air suspension at full articulation, and Australian owners run 275/65R18 LT on 18s. The OCTA fits 33s from the factory because its axles move forward slightly.
Land Rover quotes up to 3,500 kg (UK) and up to 8,200 lb (US). Owners describe the air-sprung 110 as a very stable tow vehicle because it self-levels.
900 mm (35.4 in), with Wade Sensing using the cameras to show water depth. The OCTA is quoted at one metre.

faq.q: Can I put a rooftop tent on it?
faq.a: Yes. Land Rover quotes a static roof load of up to 661 lb (300 kg) and a dynamic load of up to 370 lb on the 110 and 130 (260 lb on the 90) with off-road tyres and the Expedition Roof Rack. V8 models have no dynamic roof rating, and the OCTA's is zero in OCTA mode.
All 110 models have air as standard. The 90 can have coils or air. Coil 90s give 226 mm of ground clearance against 291 mm maximum for air, and lose the height-adjustable modes.
It has a lockable centre differential and a locking rear differential (Land Rover's Electronic Active Differential), plus brake-based torque vectoring and a two-speed transfer case.
Yes. A front-mounted 4,536 kg (10,000 lb) load-rated winch is officially supported, which is unusual for a unibody.

faq.q: How often should I change the oil?
faq.a: The headline service interval is up to 21,000 miles or two years, but Defender2.net members point out that oil changes are flagged by a separate condition-based counter, often around 15,000 miles for diesels in mixed use. Many enthusiasts change oil every 7,000–10,000 miles regardless.

US trucks launched with 2.0 four-cylinder and 3.0 six-cylinder engines, and Land Rover USA's current 110 spec page lists only the 3.0 six, with the OCTA sold as its own model. In Europe and Australia the D250/D300 diesels are the long-distance favourites, though the mild hybrids have had DC-DC converter failures and the diesels have DPF and EGR sensor faults.

It's better than its reputation off-road and worse than a Toyota in the workshop. A TFL review collected early-ownership faults, and common owner reports include DC-DC converters on MHEVs, PM/EGR sensor codes on diesels, steering knocks and several recall campaigns. Keep it on warranty or budget for a diagnostic tool and a good specialist.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Official NEDC figures range from about 7.6 L/100 km (31 mpg US) for the 3.0 diesels to 9.9 L/100 km (24 mpg US) for the P400 and 12.1 L/100 km (19 mpg US) for the P525 V8. One D300 owner reported 40 mpg (imperial) cruising at 110 km/h across France.

mods.why: Sills and rear corners are the first things a 110 hits; Terrafirma's sliders with tree bars and rear ladder are popular L663 fits.
Spare-wheel mounting kits, security and trim parts aimed squarely at the L663.
The auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes are vulnerable to stones; an Australian owner points to Offroad Animal's Toro bar as one that protects them.
BFGoodrich KO2 and General Grabber AT3 are owner favourites; the Grabber AT3 is listed in Land Rover's own iGuide and is 3PMSF-rated.
North America's big Land Rover parts house runs L663 builds, including an OCTA on 35-inch tyres with a winch bumper.

baseline_service.intro: The L663 tells you when it wants a service, but its oil-life counter and the 21,000-mile/two-year headline interval are optimistic for how most owners use their trucks, and many used examples have only ever had dealer visits. Baseline the fluids, check every recall campaign is closed, and reset the service counters with a diagnostic tool afterwards.

items.interval: Then every 7,000–10,000 mi (owner practice); oil analysis on one D300 suggested 6,000
items.note: The oil-change interval runs on its own condition-based counter, separate from the 21,000-mile service counter. Draining via the sump plug means removing the undertrays; dipstick-tube extraction works if the probe reaches the bottom.
